summary: A thirty-minute manager one-to-one. Chris opened with a welfare and pressure check on Ben's finances given collapsed lead flow, then debriefed the call Ben had taken earlier that day with a 41-year-old prospect who had sticker shock at $6,000 against a $300/month expectation and also raised a spouse objection. The diagnosis they reached together is that Ben never got a strong enough 'why' and therefore had no leverage when the price landed. Chris then role-played the whole sequence twice — first the certainty-and-isolation structure, then an escalating urgency frame built on mortality — and gave Ben a blunt piece of feedback that corroborates the pattern visible across his sales calls in this batch: he is repeatedly ending calls without deposits or commitments. Chris closed with his stated formula: a big enough problem, a big enough goal, and a strong why now.
notable: Direct managerial confirmation of the pattern this batch shows on disk: 'something's going on because you're still leaving people without deposits ... you're getting to a point where maybe you solve it and maybe you get to the end, but you're not going for getting them to actually commit.' Chris attributes it to conviction: 'typically, that is a lack of conviction on your part.'

Lead flow is materially down and management knows it: 'Leadflow is just super down. I know. I'm super aware of it ... I have a sync later with Luke to figure out what are we going to do about the leadflow.' Ben reports roughly two to three live calls for the whole week. This is essential context for any close-rate denominator over this period.

Chris opened by probing the rep's personal financial position and pressure: 'how are you doing with all of this? Financially, all of it ... are you in a place where like you really need to figure out getting on calls and getting closes?'

Ben discloses concurrent income from outside Primal Instinct: 'I've got like two clients that I'm helping build a setter teams with. So I'm getting money from that. I'm also getting money from coaching Boris's clients twice a week.'

Chris taught a mortality frame as a closing lever, role-playing it on Ben directly: 'If you knew death was coming, what would you do? Would you try or would you just accept where you're at?' → 'Let's say it was coming in a year' → 'So what do we do? Because it starts now, not tomorrow. You have 365 days.' The role play resolved with Ben saying 'send the payment link' and Chris correcting him to 'Yeah, no, actually, I'll take it on my side. What's the card number?'

Chris also gave a genuine counter-pressure caution, rejecting the confrontational version of the same move: challenging a prospect that their why is not strong enough 'tends to offend a lot of people ... considering we're about to ask you for 6k, you told them that, they're like, oh well, now they mentioned it — they probably just be like, oh yeah, I don't think it's worth 6k.'

The closest thing in the corpus to a scripted disqualification play, which the playbook currently lacks: 'I'm going to be pretty blunt with you. This is a very premium program ... they genuinely need to have a strong why and have a really strong desire to have a big transformation. If you're just looking to gain five pounds of muscle, it's just probably not going to be worth it for you.' Chris describes it as a last resort — 'it's the Hail Mary' — used only after reframing the why three or four different ways.

Stated closing philosophy worth capturing: 'I don't think objections is even the right word ... it's really more like obstacle handling', and the formula 'an obvious problem we could solve that was big enough, an obvious goal we could get them to, and a really strong why.'

Chris's stated escalation order after certainty is established: 'I would open wallet him, I would figure out a payment plan, and then I would either see if he's down to just do the payment plan. If he's giving pushback, then I would go for a deposit, and I would secure a deposit for sure.'

Chris referenced his prior sales experience selling stem cell treatments, including a $20,000 close on a 60-year-old with no strong why: 'this is genuinely just preventative for me. I'm already doing well ... Let me drop 20k.'

Ben's self-assessment of the discussed call is candid and matches the adherence picture across his other calls: he got a good pitch and no depth — 'the most important thing for these damn fitness calls, he did not give me enough' and 'this is definitely not deep enough.' He also names the swing: after going very deep with a prior prospect he consciously went shallower on this one.
